title: Extracting the anyonic exchange phase from co-tunneling through an open quantum dot
authors: Felix Puster, Matthias Thamm, Bernd Rosenow
abstract: The elementary excitations of fractional quantum Hall states obey anyonic statistics, described by an exchange phase $θ$ intermediate between the bosonic and fermionic values. We study an interferometer in which three chiral edge segments are pairwise connected by three quantum point contacts, so that, depending on the applied voltages, one of the segments acts as an open quantum dot: its spectrum is continuous, and tunneling through it is resonant without any gate tuning. This setup realizes the co-tunneling mechanism of a recently proposed antidot interferometer in a particularly simple setting. Using a non-equilibrium Keldysh calculation to third order in the tunneling amplitudes, we show that the interference current contains a co-tunneling contribution in which two quasiparticles are exchanged, so that for Laughlin states the exchange phase $θ=πν$ appears as the phase shift between the Aharonov-Bohm oscillations measured in two voltage configurations. We obtain a closed analytic expression for the interference current at finite temperature and finite separation between the quantum point contacts and show that, provided voltage-induced changes of the enclosed area are sufficiently screened, the exchange phase can be extracted from a robust phase-plateau difference. Alternatively, simultaneous measurements of the interference currents at two drains avoid this screening assumption and time-of-flight phases can be quantified analytically, allowing the exchange phase to be extracted by a controlled extrapolation with a few-percent systematic error.
summary:
This theoretical work analyzes an interferometer setup in a fractional quantum Hall state to measure the anyonic exchange phase. By calculating the co-tunneling current using a third-order Keldysh expansion, the authors demonstrate that the phase $	heta = \pi
u$ can be extracted from the interference pattern. This provides a robust theoretical pathway to probe fractional statistics using mesoscopic transport measurements.
main_problem: The paper aims to extract the anyonic exchange phase ($	heta$) characterizing fractional quantum Hall states by analyzing co-tunneling processes.
main_result:
The co-tunneling contribution to the interference current yields the exchange phase $	heta = \pi
u$ for Laughlin states, which can be extracted robustly through specific measurement configurations.
method: The analysis employs a non-equilibrium Keldysh calculation performed to third order in the tunneling amplitudes to determine the interference current.
model_or_system:
The system is an interferometer built from three chiral edge segments of a Laughlin FQH state ($
u=1/m$), connected by quantum point contacts, allowing one segment to act as an open quantum dot.
key_observables: The interference current ($I_{3,AB}$) and the resulting phase shift in Aharonov-Bohm oscillations.
important_parameters:
The filling fraction $
u$, the temperature ($T$), and the separation between the quantum point contacts.
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions involve the validity of the Luttinger liquid description and the ability to screen voltage-induced changes in the enclosed area for one extraction method.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three-segment interferometer geometry; other figures detail voltage configurations for different interference processes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical setup and theoretical framework using Luttinger liquid theory, develops the Keldysh calculation to find the co-tunneling current contribution, and finally presents two methods for extracting the phase $	heta$ from the measured interference current.
why_interesting: The use of non-equilibrium Green's functions (Keldysh formalism) to calculate transport properties in strongly correlated, topologically ordered systems like FQH states is highly relevant to open quantum systems and mesoscopic physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Interferometer formed by three chiral edge segments, each connected to its two neighbors by a QPC with tunneling amplitudes γij. On each edge, the two QPCs are separated by a distance a. Voltage biases V1, V2, and V3 are applied to sources S1, S2, and S3, respectively, and the interference current I3,AB is measured in drain D3. The Aharonov–Bohm flux through the center area between the QPCs is denoted by ϕAB. Figure taken from [82].

FIG. 2. Schematic voltage configurations relevant for the four processes. The top panel depicts the setup and voltage defi- nitions, where voltage V3 on edge 3 is used as the reference. The other panels show the tunneling paths for processes I–IV, which interfere with the reference process of direct tunneling between edges 1 and 3 to give rise to the current I3,AB. An operator O+ ij describes tunneling of a particle (blue circle) from edge i to edge j, which may leave behind a hole (white circle). FIG. 3. Region diagram for the processes at zero temperature as a function of the voltages V1 −V3 and V2 −V3 using V3 as a reference voltage. The colors show the different regions and the labels indicate the process corresponding to the region. In the lower half of the upper right quadrant and in the upper half of the lower left quadrant, a mixture of two processes occurs.

FIG. 4. Phase shift δ and amplitude ˜I of the Aharonov– Bohm dependent part of the tunneling current in drain D3, Eq. (18), as a function of V2 for different values of the voltage bias V1 −V3 with V1 = −V3 > 0. Results are shown for a temperature of 10 mK, edge velocity v = 105 m/s, and a QPC distance of a = 1 µm. For V2 ≪V3, only process I contributes and the phase shift to the Aharonov–Bohm phase shows a stable plateau at 0. For V2 ≫V1, only process II contributes such that δ plateaus at π(1/3 −1). In between the phase evolves non-monotonically. Due to the density of states anomaly, the amplitude is peaked at the Fermi levels of edges 1 and 3, V2 = ±(V1 −V3)/2.

FIG. 5. Exchange phase δ(V1, V, V3) −δ(V1, −V, V3) + π ex- tracted from plateau values obtained as in Fig. 4 at V = 80 µV as a function of the bias V1 −V3. The upper panel shows re- sults for a temperature of T = 20 mK for different QPC dis- tances a. The lower panel uses a = 1 µm and shows extracted exchange phases for different temperatures. We find that for a wide range of biases, temperature, and QPC distances, the exchange phase of π/3 can reliably be extracted.
